subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry, Year 12
about: HSC, Equilibrium, acids, organic chemistry and analysis
syllabus: NSW Chemistry Stage 6 Syllabus (2017), Year 12 course, Modules 5 to 8

points.title: Static and dynamic equilibrium
points.brief: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions go on at the same rate, so amounts stay constant. It needs a closed system.

points.title: Le Chatelier's principle
points.brief: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, it shifts to partly undo the change.

points.title: The equilibrium constant
points.brief: K is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient. A large K means products are favoured.

points.title: Temperature and the equilibrium constant
points.brief: Only temperature changes K. For an exothermic reaction, raising the temperature lowers K.

points.title: Reaction quotient
points.brief: Q has the same form as K but uses the concentrations at any moment. Comparing Q with K shows which way the reaction will move.

points.title: Dissolving ionic compounds
points.brief: When an ionic solid dissolves, water molecules surround and separate the ions. Some compounds dissolve only slightly.

points.title: The solubility product
points.brief: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for a slightly soluble salt dissolving. It is used to find solubility and predict whether a precipitate will form.

points.title: Predicting precipitation
points.brief: If the ion product is greater than Ksp, a precipitate forms.

points.title: Properties of acids and bases
points.brief: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red and react with metals and carbonates. Bases feel slippery and turn red litmus blue. Indicators change colour with pH.

points.title: Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions
points.brief: Arrhenius said acids release H⁺ ions in water. Brønsted and Lowry said an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one, which works beyond water.

points.title: Conjugate acid-base pairs
points.brief: When an acid donates a proton, what is left is its conjugate base. Strong acids have very weak conjugate bases.

points.title: Strong and weak acids
points.brief: A strong acid ionises fully in water. A weak acid ionises only partly. Strength is not the same as concentration.

points.title: pH and pOH
points.brief: pH = -log[H⁺] and pOH = -log[OH⁻], and at 25°C pH + pOH = 14.

points.title: Acid dissociation constant
points.brief: Ka measures how far a weak acid ionises, and pKa = -log Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

points.title: Neutralisation reactions
points.brief: An acid and a base react to form a salt and water, releasing heat, the enthalpy of neutralisation.

points.title: Titration
points.brief: Adding a solution of known concentration from a burette until the reaction is complete, to find an unknown concentration.

points.title: Choosing an indicator
points.brief: The indicator must change colour near the equivalence point, which depends on whether the acid and base are strong or weak.

points.title: Titration curves
points.brief: Graphs of pH against volume added, showing the equivalence point and a buffer region for weak acids.

points.title: Buffers
points.brief: A mix of a weak acid and its conjugate base resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, as blood does.

points.title: Naming hydrocarbons
points.brief: IUPAC names give the longest carbon chain, the type of bonds and where branches sit, such as 2-methylbutane.

points.title: Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
points.brief: Alkanes have only single bonds, alkenes at least one double bond and alkynes at least one triple bond.

points.title: Isomers
points.brief: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures, such as chain, position and functional group isomers.

points.title: Reactions of alkenes
points.brief: Alkenes undergo addition reactions with hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides and water. Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes, which tests for them.

points.title: Properties of hydrocarbons
points.brief: Boiling points rise with chain length because dispersion forces grow. Hydrocarbons do not dissolve in water.

points.title: Alcohols
points.brief: Alcohols have an OH group. They can be primary, secondary or tertiary, and their boiling points are higher than alkanes because of hydrogen bonding.

points.title: Reactions of alcohols
points.brief: Alcohols burn, can be dehydrated to alkenes, and are oxidised to aldehydes, ketones or carboxylic acids depending on their type.

points.title: Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids
points.brief: Aldehydes and ketones have a C=O group. Carboxylic acids have a COOH group and are weak acids.

points.title: Amines and amides
points.brief: Amines contain nitrogen and act as weak bases. Amides form when a carboxylic acid joins an amine.

points.title: Esterification
points.brief: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react, with a sulfuric acid catalyst and heat under reflux, to make an ester and water.

points.title: Soaps and detergents
points.brief: Soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, so they surround grease and lift it into water.

points.title: Addition polymers
points.brief: Alkene monomers join by opening their double bonds, as in polyethylene and PVC.

points.title: Condensation polymers
points.brief: Monomers with two functional groups join and give off a small molecule, such as water, as in nylon and polyester.

points.title: Properties and uses of polymers
points.brief: Chain length, branching and cross-links decide how strong, flexible and heat resistant a polymer is.

points.title: Why chemists analyse substances
points.brief: Analysis finds what a substance is and how much is present, for water quality, food safety, mining and health.

points.title: Tests for ions
points.brief: Flame tests and precipitation reactions identify metal ions and anions such as chloride, sulfate and carbonate.

points.title: Gravimetric analysis
points.brief: Finding the amount of a substance by making it form a precipitate, then drying and weighing it.

points.title: Atomic absorption spectroscopy
points.brief: AAS measures how much light of a set wavelength atoms absorb, to find very low concentrations of a metal. It was developed in Australia.

points.title: Colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy
points.brief: The amount of light a coloured solution absorbs rises with concentration, so a calibration curve gives an unknown concentration.

points.title: Chemical tests for organic compounds
points.brief: Simple tests identify functional groups, such as bromine water for double bonds and sodium carbonate for carboxylic acids.

points.title: Mass spectrometry
points.brief: Molecules are ionised and broken into fragments. The pattern of masses shows the molar mass and parts of the structure.

points.title: Infrared spectroscopy
points.brief: Bonds absorb infrared light at particular wavenumbers, so peaks show which functional groups are present, such as a broad O-H peak.

points.title: Carbon-13 NMR
points.brief: Each different carbon environment gives a peak, so the number of peaks shows how many kinds of carbon there are.

points.title: Proton NMR
points.brief: Peaks show the hydrogen environments, the area shows how many hydrogens, and splitting shows how many hydrogens are next door.

points.title: Designing a chemical synthesis
points.brief: Choosing reactants, conditions and steps to make a product, weighing yield, purity, cost and safety.

points.title: Yield and purity
points.brief: Percentage yield compares the product made with the most that could be made. Purity is how much of the product is the wanted substance.

points.title: Sustainability in industry
points.brief: Green chemistry aims for less waste, safer chemicals, renewable feedstocks and lower energy use.

points.title: An industrial process
points.brief: How a large-scale process, such as making ammonia by the Haber process, balances rate, yield and cost using equilibrium ideas.
